raw_text:
### Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global public health challenge, associated with high rates of hospitalization, morbidity, and mortality [1]. Despite the clinical success of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)—including renin-angiotensin-system inhibitors, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors—a significant proportion of patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) remain highly symptomatic in New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class III or IV [2]. While cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has proven highly effective for symptomatic HFrEF patients, its benefit is strictly limited to those presenting with a wide QRS complex (typically $\ge$ 130 or 150 ms, preferably with left bundle branch block morphology) [3]. This requirement leaves nearly 70% of symptomatic HF patients with a narrow QRS complex ineligible for CRT, creating a major therapeutic gap [4]. For this underserved, symptomatic "CRT-ineligible" population, cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as an innovative, device-based approach [5].

### Mechanisms of Action

Delivered via an implantable pulse generator (the Optimizer system), CCM involves the application of high-voltage, non-excitatory electrical signals during the absolute refractory period of the ventricular action potential [6]. Because these signals are delivered when the ventricular myocardium is refractory, they do not initiate a new contraction or alter the heart rate, distinguishing CCM from traditional pacing therapies [7]. Instead, CCM exerts profound biochemical and functional effects directly on the myocardium. In the acute setting, the non-excitatory signals enhance sarcoplasmic calcium dynamics by upregulating sarcoplasmic reticulum $\text{Ca}^{2+}$-ATPase (SERCA2a) and increasing the phosphorylation of phospholamban [8, 9]. Over time, these improvements in calcium handling reverse the pathological fetal gene expression program to a normal adult program, prompting left ventricular reverse remodeling, reduction in end-systolic volume, and enhanced global contractility without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption [10, 11].

### Clinical Evidence and Trials

The clinical efficacy, safety, and functional benefits of CCM have been established through a series of rigorous clinical trials. Early feasibility and randomized, double-blind trials, including the FIX-HF-4 study, demonstrated significant improvements in quality of life and exercise capacity in symptomatic HF patients [12]. The subsequent FIX-HF-5 trial confirmed these findings and identified a key subgroup of patients with a baseline left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) between 25% and 45% who derived the most pronounced benefit from CCM [13]. This finding formed the basis of the confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial, which randomized 160 patients with LVEF 25–45% and a narrow QRS complex to either CCM plus GDMT or GDMT alone [14]. Over a 24-week follow-up, CCM-treated patients showed a statistically significant improvement in peak oxygen consumption (peak $\text{VO}_2$), 6-minute walk distance (6MWD), and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire (MLHFQ) scores [14]. Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have consolidated these findings, confirming that CCM significantly improves exercise tolerance, functional status, and health-related quality of life [15, 16, 17].

### Real-world Experience, Safety, and Long-Term Outcomes

Complementing randomized trials, real-world registries and long-term cohort studies have validated the clinical safety and durability of CCM in routine clinical practice [18, 19]. Device-related complications, such as lead dislodgement, infection, or pocket hematoma, are rare and occur at rates comparable to standard pacemaker implantations [20, 21]. Crucially, long-term observational registries (e.g., the CCMR-HF registry) have shown that CCM is associated with a reduction in both all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations [22, 23]. Furthermore, clinical benefit is not restricted to patients in sinus rhythm; patients with permanent atrial fibrillation also demonstrate robust functional improvements following CCM therapy [24, 25].

### Guidelines and Future Directions

Based on the robust clinical evidence, international guidelines have recognized CCM as a viable treatment option. Both the 2016 and 2021 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines recommend considering CCM in selected patients with symptomatic HFrEF (LVEF 25–45%) despite GDMT to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life [26, 27]. Contemporary consensus statements and reviews highlight CCM as an essential option for patients who remain symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy but do not qualify for CRT [28, 29]. Moving forward, emerging pilot data suggest that CCM may also offer hemodynamic and clinical benefits in other heart failure populations, such as those with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), representing a promising avenue for future clinical trials [30].
